text:
Create a Quarto Document for Publishing
In this exercise you will create a publication-quality document using a PLOS journal template, run a gene variability analysis, and generate a heatmap figure.

Setup

Check whether you have the following packages installed:

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(scales)
If any are missing, install them in your console:
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("readxl")
install.packages("scales")






TipChecking installed packages in Positron



You can also check in the Extensions pane by searching for the package name.




Install the PLOS Template

In your Terminal tab, run the following commands one at a time:

quarto add quarto-journals/plos
quarto use template quarto-journals/plos






NoteWhat this does



This installs a Quarto extension that formats your document to match PLOS journal submission requirements — including layout, fonts, and figure formatting. This is the same approach used for many other journal templates available through quarto-journals.




Gene Variability Analysis

Copy the code below and paste it into your publication.qmd file underneath the heading ## Gene Variability Analysis. Start your code block with ```{r} and close it with ```.







NoteAbout the #| lines



These are chunk options — they tell Quarto how to handle the output when this code runs inside a .qmd file. message: false suppresses package loading messages, and warning: false suppresses warnings.


#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Prepare data - rename the first column and use both ID columns
gene_data_long <- gene_data %>%
  rename(ensembl_id = `...1`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gene_symbol), gene_symbol != "") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(ensembl_id, gene_symbol),
               names_to = "sample",
               values_to = "expression")

# Calculate variance for each gene across all samples
gene_variability <- gene_data_long %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol, ensembl_id) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_expression        = mean(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance               = var(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    coefficient_of_variation = sd(expression, na.rm = TRUE) / mean_expression,
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Identify top 15 most variable genes
top_genes <- gene_variability %>%
  arrange(desc(variance)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

# Display summary statistics
cat("Total genes analyzed:", nrow(gene_variability), "\n")
cat("Mean variance across all genes:",
    round(mean(gene_variability$variance, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
cat("Most variable gene:", top_genes$gene_symbol[1],
    "with variance =", round(top_genes$variance[1], 2), "\n")

# Show the top 10 most variable genes
cat("\nTop 10 most variable genes:\n")
print(top_genes %>%
        select(gene_symbol, variance) %>%
        slice_head(n = 10) %>%
        mutate(variance = round(variance, 2)))


Data Visualization

Copy the code below and paste it into your publication.qmd file underneath the heading ## Data Visualization. Start your code block with ```{r} and close it with ```.

#| fig-cap: "Expression heatmap showing scaled expression levels of the
#|   15 most variable genes across all samples. Blue indicates
#|   below-average expression, white indicates average expression,
#|   and red indicates above-average expression for each gene."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

# Prepare heatmap data
heatmap_data <- gene_data_long %>%
  filter(gene_symbol %in% top_genes$gene_symbol) %>%
  left_join(top_genes %>% select(gene_symbol, variance),
            by = "gene_symbol") %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  mutate(scaled_expr = scale(expression)[, 1]) %>%
  ungroup()

# Create heatmap visualization
expression_heatmap <- heatmap_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample,
             y = reorder(gene_symbol, variance),
             fill = scaled_expr)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low   = "blue",
    mid   = "white",
    high  = "red",
    name  = "Scaled\nExpression",
    limits = c(-3, 3),
    oob   = scales::squish
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Expression Variability Heatmap: Top 15 Most Variable Genes",
    subtitle = "Genes ordered by variance (highest at top)",
    x        = "Sample ID",
    y        = "Gene Symbol"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x  = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
    axis.text.y  = element_text(size = 10, face = "italic"),
    plot.title   = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid   = element_blank()
  )

print(expression_heatmap)

# Save high-resolution figure
ggsave(paste0("outputs/", timestamp, "_expression_heatmap.png"),
       plot   = expression_heatmap,
       width  = 10,
       height = 6,
       dpi    = 300)

Render your publication.qmd document to see your PLOS-formatted article







TipSaving your figure



Notice the ggsave() call at the end of the visualization block. This saves a high-resolution .png to your outputs/ folder with a timestamp in the filename — the same automated file naming pattern introduced in the Project Management section.

text:
Quick background

Base R (no packages)

This is the original, old school way of reading .csv, .txt, and .dat files and returns a data frame in the R environment using the function read.csv, read.table, etc.
Cumbersome - it requires additional manual coding specifications based on the file type; it can be slow for large datasets; and can lead to unexpected behaviors with certain column types (i.e. converting character columns into factors)



readr package

Modern alternative to Base R and requires less configuration while being faster, cleaner, and provides less coding headaches (its does not convert character columns into factors) and uses the function read_csv, read_tsv, etc.
Returns a tibble, a modern data frame with features that make it print nicely, displays on a screen better, does not change variables names, and does not use row labels. The output when inspecting the data set using str() are nicer looking and more informative







Noteread_csv() vs read.csv()



This section uses read_csv() from the Tidyverse rather than read.csv() from base R. Key differences:



Feature
read_csv()
read.csv()




Column types
Explicit (col_double, etc.)
Inferred


Speed
Faster on large files
Slower

Tibble
Data frame

May be altered


Row labels
Not used
Supported



A tibble is a modern data frame that prints more cleanly, displays better on screen, and produces more informative output from functions like str().




haven package

The haven package is the dedicated tool for reading proprietary formats like SPSS (.sav), SAS (.xpt & .sas7bdat), and Stata (.dta), and is a key part of the Tidyverse ecosystem.



openxlsx package

The openxlsx package is the dedicated tool for reading and writing data from Excel files (.xlsx) without needing external dependencies like Java. It is widely used for working with multi-sheet workbooks, applying styles, and handling complex Excel features, offering functions like read.xlsx() for import.

Is highly useful because it provides a single, universal function for importing virtually any data file format.
The import() function automatically detects the file type based on the file extension (e.g., .csv, .xlsx, .RData, .rds, .xpt, .sas7bdat, .dta, .sav, .json,.txt, .dat) and uses the appropriate specialized package (readr,haven, and openxlsx) to import it.



here package

The package here and its function here() make it easy to tell R where to find and to save your files - in essence, it builds file paths.
Using here() works with you R Project to eliminate path problems -> Relative paths = good for sharing; Absolute paths = Bad for sharing

Bad: "/Users/mwegener/Desktop/maybe_here/data.csv"
Good: here("raw_data", "data.csv")

The tidyverse is a collection of R packages designed around shared principles for efficient, readable data analysis. Install all packages at once with install.packages("tidyverse") and load with library(tidyverse).

Core Philosophy:

Tidy data structure: Each variable = column, each observation = row, each value = cell
Consistent syntax: Predictable function behavior across all packages
Human-centered design: Intuitive functions that reduce learning curve

Uniform data structures using data frames/tibbles
Reproducible analysis with version control emphasis
Clean naming conventions (lowercase_with_underscores)
Active community support and best practices
Functional pipelines that transform data through logical steps

title: Finding Differentially Expressed Genes with DESeq2
text:
Part 1 — Setup

1.1 Load Required Packages

library(here)
library(DESeq2)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(apeglm)     # used by lfcShrink() in Part 7







Note



apeglm is loaded here even though we never call it directly — lfcShrink() reaches it via type = "apeglm". Because that’s a string, renv cannot see the dependency when it scans your code, so without this library() call renv::snapshot() leaves apeglm out of the lockfile and Part 7 fails for anyone who restores from it. Same reasoning for tibble, used as tibble::rownames_to_column().




1.2 Define File Paths
Why use here::here()? Using here() makes your paths relative to the project root, so the script works on any machine regardless of where the project folder is saved. This is especially important when sharing code via GitHub.

# In your own ShankProject the cleaned data sits at <project root>/processed_data,
# which is the first branch below. This page is published from the ARCS website
# repository, where the same two files ship alongside the workshop materials —
# the fallback keeps the published version reproducible without changing the
# path you would write in your own project.
dir_data <- if (dir.exists(here("processed_data"))) {
  here("processed_data")
} else {
  here("workshops", "apptainer", "_materials", "processed_data")
}

dir_out <- if (dir.exists(here("processed_data"))) {
  here("outputs")
} else {
  here("workshops", "arcs_04", "_materials", "outputs")
}

# Input paths
path_counts   <- file.path(dir_data, "Shank3_rawCounts_clean.csv")
path_metadata <- file.path(dir_data, "Shank3_metadata_clean.csv")

# Output paths
path_figures <- file.path(dir_out, "figures")
path_tables  <- file.path(dir_out, "tables")

# Create output folders if they do not exist yet
for (dir in c(path_figures, path_tables)) {
  if (!dir.exists(dir)) {
    dir.create(dir, recursive = TRUE)
    cat("✅ Created:", dir, "\n")
  }
}

section: ✂️ Part 3 — Subset to a Simple Two-Group Comparison
text:
✂️ Part 3 — Subset to a Simple Two-Group Comparison
Why subset? The full dataset contains samples from two conditions (normal and sleep-deprived) and two genotypes (WT and Shank3).
For this workshop we focus on a simple two-group comparison: Shank3 vs WT, using only the normal condition samples. This keeps the design formula simple and the results easier to interpret.

3.1 Keep only samples from the normal (baseline) condition

info_sub <- clean_info %>% filter(condition == "normal")



3.2 Subset counts to matching samples

counts_sub <- clean_counts[, info_sub$sample_id]



3.3 Drop unused factor levels after subsetting

info_sub$genotype <- droplevels(info_sub$genotype)



3.4 Set WT as the reference level (baseline for comparison)

info_sub$genotype <- relevel(info_sub$genotype, ref = "WT")



3.5 Confirm subset dimensions

cat("Subsetted dataset:", nrow(counts_sub), "genes x", ncol(counts_sub), "samples\n")

Subsetted dataset: 28886 genes x 10 samples

title: Finding Differentially Expressed Genes with DESeq2
text:
🏗️ Part 4 — Build the DESeq2 Object

4.1 Create DESeqDataSet

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = counts_sub,   # genes x samples count matrix
  colData   = info_sub,     # sample metadata
  design    = ~ genotype    # simple two-group design
)







NoteUnderstanding the design formula



~ genotype tells DESeq2 to model gene expression as a function of genotype.
With WT set as the reference, all results will be expressed as Shank3 relative to WT.




4.2 Pre-filter Low-Count Genes
Keep genes with at least 10 counts in at least 3 samples (adjust thresholds based on your smallest group size).

keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3
dds  <- dds[keep, ]

cat("Genes remaining after filtering:", nrow(dds), "\n")

Genes remaining after filtering: 15742

title: Finding Differentially Expressed Genes with DESeq2
text:
🔬 Part 5 — Run DESeq2

dds <- DESeq(dds)







NoteWhat does DESeq() do?



Three steps happen automatically:

Size factor estimation — normalizes for differences in sequencing depth
Dispersion estimation — models count variability across samples
Model fitting — fits a negative binomial GLM and tests each gene

title: Finding Differentially Expressed Genes with DESeq2
text:
📊 Part 6 — Quality Control

6.1 Transform Counts for Visualization
vst = Variance Stabilizing Transformation. It is faster than rlog() for larger datasets; both are suitable for QC.

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)







Noteblind = TRUE vs blind = FALSE




blind = TRUE — the transformation ignores the design (used for QC and exploration)
blind = FALSE — the transformation uses the design (used for downstream visualization of results)





6.2 PCA Plot






TipWhat to look for in the PCA




Samples should cluster by genotype along PC1 (the axis of greatest variation)
Any outlier samples should be investigated before proceeding
If genotype is not the dominant source of variation, review your metadata




pca_data <- plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "genotype", returnData = TRUE)

pct_var <- round(100 * attr(pca_data, "percentVar"))

pca_plot <- ggplot(pca_data, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = genotype, label = name)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("WT" = "#2196F3", "Shank3" = "#F44336")) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA: Shank3 vs WT (normal condition)",
    x = paste0("PC1: ", pct_var[1], "% variance"),
    y = paste0("PC2: ", pct_var[2], "% variance")
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

pca_plot




PCA of variance-stabilized counts, coloured by genotype.



# Save
ggsave(
  filename = file.path(path_figures, "PCA_Shank3vsWT.png"),
  plot = pca_plot, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300
)



6.3 Sample Distance Heatmap

samp_dists <- dist(t(assay(vsd)))
samp_mat   <- as.matrix(samp_dists)

rownames(samp_mat) <- colnames(samp_mat) <-
  paste(colData(vsd)$genotype, colData(vsd)$sample_id, sep = " | ")

colors <- colorRampPalette(rev(brewer.pal(9, "Blues")))(255)

# Display inline
pheatmap(samp_mat, col = colors,
         clustering_distance_rows = samp_dists,
         clustering_distance_cols = samp_dists,
         main = "Sample-to-Sample Distances",
         fontsize = 10)




Euclidean distances between samples, computed on the variance-stabilized counts.



# Save to file
pheatmap(samp_mat, col = colors,
         clustering_distance_rows = samp_dists,
         clustering_distance_cols = samp_dists,
         main = "Sample-to-Sample Distances", fontsize = 10,
         filename = file.path(path_figures, "SampleDistances_Shank3vsWT.png"))

📈 Part 7 — Extract & Interpret Results

7.1 Check Available Coefficients

resultsNames(dds)

[1] "Intercept"             "genotype_Shank3_vs_WT"




7.2 Extract Results: Shank3 vs WT

# alpha sets the FDR threshold used for independent filtering
res <- results(dds, name = "genotype_Shank3_vs_WT", alpha = 0.05)

summary(res)


out of 15742 with nonzero total read count
adjusted p-value < 0.05
LFC > 0 (up)       : 10, 0.064%
LFC < 0 (down)     : 6, 0.038%
outliers [1]       : 1, 0.0064%
low counts [2]     : 0, 0%
(mean count < 3)
[1] see 'cooksCutoff' argument of ?results
[2] see 'independentFiltering' argument of ?results








NoteUnderstanding the results columns










Column
Meaning




baseMean
Average normalized count across all samples


log2FoldChange
Log2 ratio of Shank3 / WT


lfcSE
Standard error of the log2 fold change


stat
Wald test statistic


pvalue
Raw p-value


padj
Adjusted p-value (FDR) — use this for significance testing







7.3 Shrink Fold Changes (Recommended)

# lfcShrink improves fold change estimates for genes with low counts.
# This is recommended for ranking and visualization — NOT for hypothesis testing.

res_shrunk <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "genotype_Shank3_vs_WT", type = "apeglm")

summary(res_shrunk)


out of 15742 with nonzero total read count
adjusted p-value < 0.1
LFC > 0 (up)       : 13, 0.083%
LFC < 0 (down)     : 10, 0.064%
outliers [1]       : 1, 0.0064%
low counts [2]     : 0, 0%
(mean count < 3)
[1] see 'cooksCutoff' argument of ?results
[2] see 'independentFiltering' argument of ?results








TipWhy shrink fold changes?



Genes with low counts can have artificially extreme fold changes due to high variability. lfcShrink() pulls these estimates towards zero, making volcano plots and ranked gene lists more reliable.
Use res_shrunk for visualization. Use res for hypothesis testing.




7.4 MA Plot

# Save to file
png(file.path(path_figures, "MAplot_Shank3vsWT.png"),
    width = 700, height = 500, res = 120)

plotMA(res_shrunk, ylim = c(-5, 5),
       main      = "MA Plot: Shank3 vs WT",
       alpha     = 0.1,
       colSig    = "#F44336",
       colNonSig = "grey60")

invisible(dev.off())

# Display inline
plotMA(res_shrunk, ylim = c(-5, 5),
       main      = "MA Plot: Shank3 vs WT",
       alpha     = 0.1,
       colSig    = "#F44336",
       colNonSig = "grey60")




MA plot showing log2 fold change (Shank3/WT) versus mean expression. Significant genes are highlighted in red.






7.5 Volcano Plot

res_df <- as.data.frame(res_shrunk) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("gene") %>%
  filter(!is.na(padj)) %>%
  mutate(
    significance = case_when(
      padj < 0.1 & log2FoldChange > 0 ~ "Up in Shank3",
      padj < 0.1 & log2FoldChange < 0 ~ "Down in Shank3",
      TRUE                            ~ "Not significant"
    )
  )

deg_counts <- table(res_df$significance)
deg_counts


 Down in Shank3 Not significant    Up in Shank3 
             10           15718              13 

volcano_plot <- ggplot(res_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = significance)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Up in Shank3"    = "#F44336",
    "Down in Shank3"  = "#2196F3",
    "Not significant" = "grey70"
  )) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(
    title = "Volcano Plot: Shank3 vs WT",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Up: ", deg_counts["Up in Shank3"],
      " | Down: ", deg_counts["Down in Shank3"]
    ),
    x = "Log2 Fold Change (Shank3 / WT)",
    y = "-Log10 Adjusted P-value",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

volcano_plot




Volcano plot of adjusted significance against effect size.



ggsave(file.path(path_figures, "Volcano_Shank3vsWT.png"),
       plot = volcano_plot, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)

The problem: “it works on my machine”

Your analysis runs perfectly… on your laptop
A collaborator runs the same code and it breaks
Different R version, different package version, different OS
Reproducible research can’t depend on whose computer it is

title:

Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
What is a container?
A single file that packages your entire computing environment:

the R installation
every package, at a pinned version
the system libraries underneath


Run that file anywhere → get exactly that environment.

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
More than pinning packages

renv pins your R packages — good instinct, one layer up
But it still assumes R is installed, at a compatible version, on an OS with the right system libraries
A container ships all of it


renv is the shopping list. The container is the groceries.

title:

Programming in R Part 4:

text:
Not a virtual machine









Virtual machine
Container




Simulates
A whole computer + kernel
Nothing — shares the host kernel


Size
Gigabytes of overhead
Just your software


Start-up
Boots like a machine
Seconds, like a command




Containers borrow the Linux kernel — they don’t simulate one.
That’s why Apptainer needs Linux.

text:
Four words to keep straight







Term
What it is




Container
The idea: software packaged with all it needs


Image .sif
The file on disk — one shareable artifact


Apptainer
The program that builds and runs images


Definition .def
The text recipe for an image




Write a .def → Apptainer builds an image → Apptainer runs it.
Today: only the last step.

title:

text:
So what is Apptainer?

Note0 vs. NA — these are not the same thing





It’s tempting to treat 0 as a stand-in for “nothing” — but in R, 0 is a real, known value, while NA means unknown or not recorded. A newborn family member who is 0 years old is a known fact. text:
ℹ️ About This






ImportantThe project is the unit of reproducibility





It’s tempting to think of a single script as “the analysis.” But a script alone can’t be reproduced — it depends on data files, package versions, and a folder structure that has to exist for it to run. The project, not the script, is what makes your work reproducible: the folders, the renv.lock, the raw data, and the code together. If you zipped your project folder and sent it to a stranger, could they run it? That’s the real test.









NoteWhy does the Build block download the data, but the Code Tour reads it straight from a URL?





This isn’t an inconsistency — it’s intentional. In a real project, raw data should live inside your project folder (raw_data/) so your analysis doesn’t silently depend on the internet being available every time you run it. If the GitHub repo moves, is renamed, or GitHub has an outage, a project with a local copy still runs. A project that re-fetches a URL every time does not.
Browser-based tools like webR can’t save a persistent local copy the way a laptop can, so reading from the URL each time is the necessary workaround for that environment — not the ideal pattern. You’re seeing a real technical tradeoff, not a mistake.

Caution🟠 Code Tour — Why Didn’t My Answer Update?





Change my_age and re-run only that one line:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
birth_year still shows the old value — because R doesn’t recalculate it automatically. It only stores what you told it to store, at the moment you ran that line. The variable has no memory of how it was created, only what it currently holds.
This is a small version of a problem that shows up everywhere in computational work: a pipeline is only as current as the last time each step was actually re-run. Changing one upstream value — a raw data point, a filtering threshold, a parameter — doesn’t automatically update everything downstream of it. You have to re-run the whole chain, in order, every time.
This is why, later in ARCS, you’ll get in the habit of re-running entire scripts top to bottom rather than just the last line you touched — and it’s part of why reproducibility isn’t only “did I get the right answer,” but “would I get the same answer again if I changed one thing and reran everything downstream of it?”

text:
Setup Steps
Complete as many of these as you can before Session 1, in order. Stop wherever you get stuck and bring your questions to class — or reach out to us in advance using the contact information at the bottom of this page.


Step 1: Install R
R is the statistical computing language we will use throughout the series.
Windows and Mac:

Go to cran.r-project.org
Click your operating system
Download the latest installer
Run the installer using all default options

Windows only — also install Rtools:
After installing R, go to the Rtools page on CRAN and download the version that matches your R installation (e.g., Rtools44 for R 4.4). Run the installer using default options.
Mac only — also install Command Line Tools:
Open the Terminal application (search for “Terminal” in Spotlight) and run:
xcode-select --install
A dialog box will appear — click Install and follow the prompts.






Note



📘 About This: Why Both R and Rtools/Command Line Tools?
R is the language. Rtools (Windows) and Command Line Tools (Mac) are compilers that allow R to build certain packages from source code — including several packages we use in this series. You will not interact with them directly, but R needs them to be present.


Step 2: Create a GitHub Account
GitHub is where we will store and share our work. You will need a free account.
Go to github.com and click Sign up
Enter your email address, create a password, and choose a username
Verify your account using the code GitHub sends to your email
You can skip the personalization questions at the end
Keep a note of your username and password — you will need them in Step 3. Step 3: Install GitHub Desktop
GitHub Desktop is a visual application that makes it easier to work with Git and GitHub without using the command line.
Windows:
Go to desktop.github.com
Click Download for Windows (64-bit)
Run the downloaded .exe file — it will install and open automatically
Sign in with the GitHub account you created in Step 2
Mac:
Go to desktop.github.com
Click Download for macOS
Open the downloaded .zip file — this extracts the GitHub Desktop app
Drag GitHub Desktop into your Applications folder
Open it from Applications and sign in with your GitHub account
Step 4: Get the Course Data
We will use the same dataset throughout the series. Clone the course data repository using GitHub Desktop:
Make sure GitHub Desktop is open and you are signed in
Visit this URL in your browser: https://github.com/CWML/arcs-data
Click the green Code button
Select Open with GitHub Desktop
When GitHub Desktop opens, choose a location you can find easily (Desktop or Documents) and click Clone
This downloads a folder called arcs-data containing the two data files we will use. You do not need to do anything else with this folder yet — we will use it in Session 1.






Note



📘 About This: Why Clone Instead of Just Downloading?
We clone the data repository rather than downloading a zip file so that you practice the same workflow you will use throughout the series. Cloning also makes it easy to get any updates we push before future sessions.


Step 5: Install Positron
Positron is the IDE (integrated development environment) we will use to write and run R code. It was built by Posit specifically for data science work.
Go to the Positron releases page on GitHub
Find the most recent stable release
Under Assets, download the installer for your operating system:
    Windows: .exe file
    Mac: .dmg file
Run the installer
Open Positron — it should automatically detect your R installation and show R in the bottom right corner






Important



⚠️ Watch Out
If Positron does not detect R automatically, go to Settings → R and point it to your R installation manually. On Mac this is usually /usr/local/bin/R or /opt/homebrew/bin/R. On Windows it is usually C:Files-4.x.x.exe.


Step 6: Open the Course Repository in Positron
Once Positron is installed:
Open Positron
Go to File → Open Folder
Navigate to the arcs-data folder you cloned in Step 4
Click Open
Positron will restart in project mode. You should see the folder contents in the file explorer panel on the left.

Why Project Management Matters
A consistent project structure means a collaborator — or you, six months from now — can open your folder and immediately understand what goes where, without asking you a single question. This is one piece of what we mean by reproducibility






Important🔴 For Browser-Based Students





The folder structure, renv, and README steps below require a persistent filesystem — something a browser sandbox can’t provide. Directories created in webR exist only for this page session and disappear on refresh.
Read through these steps to understand why a reproducible project needs them, but you’ll need a local R install (Positron or RStudio) to actually build and keep a project folder. The dataset-loading steps further down do work live in your browser, since they don’t depend on anything being saved.

Build Your Folder Structure

dir.create("raw_data")
dir.create("processed_data")
dir.create("scripts")
dir.create("outputs")




Folder
Purpose




raw_data/
Original data. Never edit these files directly.


processed_data/
Cleaned, transformed versions of your data.


scripts/
Your code.


outputs/
Figures, tables, and results.









Caution🟠 Code Tour — File Naming Conventions






No spaces — use _ or - instead
Start timestamped files with an ISO date: YYYY-MM-DD
Be descriptive

Avoid: - ❌ data analysis.R (spaces) - ❌ data.csv (not descriptive) - ❌ final_FINAL_really_final.R (version chaos)
Prefer: - ✅ 2024-03-15_survey_analysis.R - ✅ participant_demographics_clean.csv - ✅ README.md

title: Arc 2: Your First Reproducible Project
text:
Initialize renv
renv tracks exactly which package versions your project uses, so it runs the same way on any machine, including yours a year from now.

renv::init()
renv::snapshot()

This creates:
├── .Rprofile
├── renv.lock
└── renv/
    ├── .gitignore
    ├── activate.R
    ├── settings.json
    └── library/






Note🟣 Learn More — What’s actually inside renv.lock?





{
  "R": { "Version": "4.6.0" },
  "Packages": {
    "dplyr": {
      "Package": "dplyr",
      "Version": "1.1.4",
      "Source": "Repository"
    }
  }
}
Every package your project depends on gets pinned to an exact version here. When a collaborator runs renv::restore(), R installs these exact versions — not whatever happens to be newest that day. The full renv documentation is at rstudio.github.io/renv.

text:
Load the Dataset
We’ll use this dataset — real RNA-seq data from a published Shank3 mouse study — for the rest of the series.

# ---- Download once, save locally ----
metadata_url  <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv"
rawcounts_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv"

download.file(metadata_url,  destfile = "raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
download.file(rawcounts_url, destfile = "raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")

metadata  <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
rawcounts <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")

# ---- For browser-based students only: uncomment the lines below ----
# metadata  <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
# rawcounts <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")

Inspect what you loaded:

head(metadata)
str(metadata)
dim(rawcounts)







Note⚪ About This — Why download-and-save here, but read-from-URL in the Code Tour below?





This isn’t an inconsistency — it’s intentional. In a real project, raw data should live inside your project folder (raw_data/) so your analysis doesn’t silently depend on the internet being available every time you run it. If the GitHub repo moves, is renamed, or GitHub has an outage, a project with a local copy still runs. A project that re-fetches a URL every time does not.
Browser-based tools like webR can’t save a persistent local copy the way a laptop can, so reading from the URL each time is the necessary workaround for that environment — not the ideal pattern. You’re seeing a real technical tradeoff, not a mistake.

Note🟣 Learn More — README Templates





This project’s README is a simplified version of the Cornell Research Data Management README template: Cornell eCommons README Template









Note⚪ About This — The project is the unit of reproducibility





It’s tempting to think of a single script as “the analysis.” But a script alone can’t be reproduced — it depends on data files, package versions, and a folder structure that has to exist for it to run. The project, not the script, is what makes your work reproducible: the folders, the renv.lock, the raw data, and the code together. If you zipped your project folder and sent it to a stranger, could they run it? That’s the real test.

text:
Two Basic Rules for Writing Reproducible Code

Use # to annotate and document your code. A comment explains why you did something, not just what the code does — that’s the difference between code you can hand to someone else and code only you can decode.
Use a visible pattern to separate sections, e.g. #----- Section Title ------#. This turns a script into something a collaborator — or you, in six months — can scan and navigate without reading every line.

These two habits are the first, smallest form of reproducibility: a reader who wasn’t there when you wrote the code should still be able to follow your thinking.

Argument

Assignment Operator

Setup Steps


Step 1: Install R
R is the computing language we will use throughout the series.
Windows and Mac:

Go to cran.r-project.org
Click your operating system
Download the latest installer
Run the installer using all default options

Windows only — also install Rtools:
After installing R, go to the Rtools page on CRAN and download the version that matches your R installation (e.g., Rtools44 for R 4.4). Run the installer using default options.
Mac only — also install Command Line Tools:
Open the Terminal application (search for “Terminal” in Spotlight) and run:
xcode-select --install
A dialog box will appear — click Install and follow the prompts.






Note About This — Why Both R and Rtools/Command Line Tools?



R is the language. Rtools (Windows) and Command Line Tools (Mac) are compilers that allow R to build certain packages from source code — including several packages we use in this series. You will not interact with them directly, but R needs them to be present.




Step 2: Create a GitHub Account
GitHub is where we will store and share our work. You will need a free account.

Go to github.com and click Sign up
Enter your email address, create a password, and choose a username
Verify your account using the code GitHub sends to your email
You can skip the personalization questions at the end

Keep a note of your username and password — you will need them in Step 3.


Step 3: Install GitHub Desktop
GitHub Desktop is a visual application that makes it easier to work with Git and GitHub without using the command line.
Windows:

Go to desktop.github.com
Click Download for Windows (64-bit)
Run the downloaded .exe file — it will install and open automatically
Sign in with the GitHub account you created in Step 2

Mac:

Go to desktop.github.com
Click Download for macOS
Open the downloaded .zip file — this extracts the GitHub Desktop app
Drag GitHub Desktop into your Applications folder
Open it from Applications and sign in with your GitHub account



Step 4: Get the Course Data
We will use the same dataset throughout the series. Clone the course data repository using GitHub Desktop:

Make sure GitHub Desktop is open and you are signed in
Visit this URL in your browser: https://github.com/CWML/arcs-data #TODO update URL
Click the green Code button
Select Open with GitHub Desktop
When GitHub Desktop opens, choose a location you can find easily (Desktop or Documents) and click Clone

This downloads a folder called arcs-data #TODO updatecontaining the two data files we will use. You do not need to do anything else with this folder yet — we will use it in Session 1.






Note About This — Why Clone Instead of Just Downloading?



We clone the data repository rather than downloading a zip file so that you practice the same workflow you will use throughout the series. Cloning also makes it easy to get any updates we push before future sessions.




Step 5: Install Positron
Positron is the IDE (integrated development environment) we will use to write and run R code. It was built by Posit specifically for data science work.

Go to the Positron releases page on GitHub
Find the most recent stable release

Run the installer

Important Watch Out



If Positron does not detect R automatically, go to Settings → R and point it to your R installation manually. On Mac this is usually /usr/local/bin/R or /opt/homebrew/bin/R. On Windows it is usually C:\Program Files\R\R-4.x.x\bin\R.exe.

Go to File → Open Folder

Arithmetic
R evaluates arithmetic the way you’d expect from paper math:

One syntax rule worth knowing up front: text must be wrapped in quotation marks " " — object names are the only exception. Watch what happens when you “forget”. Run Hello world! on its own, then run "Hello world!" in quotes.






Caution Code Tour — Why does one of these fail?





Hello world!
R reads this as an attempt to call an object named Hello — but Hello has never been created, and world! isn’t valid syntax either. You’ll see an error like unexpected symbol. Wrapping it in quotes tells R “this is text, not code”:
"Hello world!"
Error messages like this will come up constantly — learning to read them calmly is a core programming skill, not a sign something’s gone wrong.

text:
Objects and Assignment
R stores information in objects using the assignment arrow <-.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Caution Code Tour — Why Didn’t My Answer Update?





Change my_age and re-run only that one line:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
birth_year still shows the old value — because R doesn’t recalculate it automatically. It only stores what you told it to store, at the moment you ran that line. The variable has no memory of how it was created, only what it currently holds.
This is a small version of a problem that shows up everywhere in computational work: a pipeline is only as current as the last time each step was actually re-run. Changing one upstream value — a raw data point, a filtering threshold, a parameter — doesn’t automatically update everything downstream of it. You have to re-run the whole chain, in order, every time.
This is why, later in ARCS, you’ll get in the habit of re-running entire scripts top to bottom rather than just the last line you touched — and it’s part of why reproducibility isn’t only “did I get the right answer,” but “would I get the same answer again if I changed one thing and reran everything downstream of it?”









Note Learn More — Object Naming Rules






Must start with a letter (not a number or symbol)
Can contain letters, numbers, _ and .
Case-sensitive: age and Age are different objects
Avoid names that are already functions in R (e.g. c, mean, data)

Why Project Management Matters
A consistent project structure means a collaborator — or you, six months from now — can open your folder and immediately understand what goes where, without asking you a single question. This is one piece of what we mean by reproducibility.

Read through these steps to understand why a reproducible project needs them, but you’ll need a local R install (Positron or RStudio) to actually build and keep a project folder. Note About This — Minimal Packages, On Purpose





Base R ships with a core set of built-in [functions](/glossary.qmd#function). A [package](/glossary.qmd#package) is an add-on that extends what R can do — installed once per machine with install.packages(), then turned on for each new R session with library(). The very next tool we use, renv, is a package — and it needs to be installed before it can do anything.
This series installs very few packages before Arc 5. That’s deliberate: the goal here is understanding what a package actually does for you — renv protects reproducibility, fs generates a file tree.

Tip Learn More — What’s Actually Inside renv.lock?

We’ll use this dataset — real RNA-seq data from a published Shank3 mouse study — for the rest of the series. Two files: a raw counts matrix, and a metadata file describing each sample. We’ll call them raw_data and raw_metadata throughout, matching the raw_data/ folder they live in.

Inspect what you loaded:

str(raw_metadata)
dim(raw_data)







Note About This — Why Download-and-Save Here, but Read-from-URL Below?





This isn’t an inconsistency — it’s intentional. In a real project, raw data should live inside your project folder (raw_data/) so your analysis doesn’t silently depend on the internet being available every time you run it. If the GitHub repo moves, is renamed, or GitHub has an outage, a project with a local copy still runs. A project that re-fetches a URL every time does not.
Browser-based tools like webR can’t save a persistent local copy the way a laptop can, so reading from the URL each time is the necessary workaround for that environment — not the ideal pattern. You’re seeing a real technical tradeoff, not a mistake.

text:
Vectors, Matrices, Data Frames — and Lists

Vector — one type of value, in a line.
Matrix — one type of value, in rows and columns.
Data frame — mixed types allowed, organized in rows and columns; this is what most of your data will look like.
List — the most flexible structure: can hold anything, including other lists, vectors, or data frames, all at once.

title: Arc 3
text:

A script that only works once, on one exact dataset, isn’t reproducible — it’s lucky.
Functions let you package a calculation so you don’t repeat it.
Loops let you repeat an action without copy-pasting.
Conditionals let your code respond differently depending on what it finds.
Together, these are what let a script survive contact with messier, real data.

Static vs. Dynamic Documents
A static script produces output once:

mean_x <- mean(data$x)
# Output: 42.5

If the data changes, the report is now wrong.
If the analysis changes, you have to remember to update the write-up separately.

What Is a Package?

R packages are collections of functions and data that extend base R.
Installed once with install.packages(), loaded each session with library().
Created and shared by a global community of users — not by any single authority.

title: Arc 5
text:
Why Tidy Data?

Tidy data principle: each variable in a column, each observation in a row, each value in a cell.
The tidyverse is a collection of packages built around that one shared shape — so once your data is tidy, every tool in the family works the same way.
dplyr gives you a grammar for this: select(), filter(), mutate(), arrange(), summarize(), group_by().
The pipe (%>%) chains these into a readable sequence of steps, read top to bottom.

title: Arc 5
text:
Meet R Where It’s At

Popular doesn’t mean limitation-free.
Tidyverse functions are opinionated — they assume your data is already (or can become) tidy.
Knowing when a tool fits, and when it doesn’t, is part of using it responsibly.

Back in Arc 1, we said R is flexible — and that flexibility creates responsibility.
You’ve felt this by now: code ran, functions worked, but you decided whether the output made sense.
Packages don’t remove that responsibility. They just change its shape.

text:
AI Can Write Code — Who Checks It?

AI-generated code can run without error and still be wrong — statistically, biologically, or just quietly.
Everything you’ve learned (functions, error messages, Git history, renv.lock) is exactly the toolkit for verifying code you didn’t write yourself.
The habits don’t change. Only who typed the first draft does.

The repo is the reproducible artifact — whether you wrote every line of it or not.
Code, environment, and data now travel together, with a record of how they got that way.

title: Arc 7
text:
Your Code, Someone Else’s Machine

A shared repo and a locked renv.lock still leave one thing unaddressed: the operating system underneath.
Containers package the entire environment — OS included.

title: Arc 7
text:
Containers vs. Virtual Machines

A virtual machine simulates an entire computer, including its own OS kernel — heavy, slow to start.
A container shares the host’s Linux kernel and packages only what sits above it — software, libraries, files.
That’s why a container starts in seconds, and why it needs Linux specifically: it isn’t simulating a kernel, it’s borrowing the one already running.

section: Create a Quarto Document for Publishing
text:
Create a Quarto Document for Publishing
In this exercise you will create a publication-quality document using a PLOS journal template, run a gene variability analysis, and generate a heatmap figure.

Setup
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(scales)
# if any are missing: install.packages("tidyverse"); install.packages("readxl"); install.packages("scales")






TipChecking installed packages in Positron



You can also check in the Extensions pane by searching for the package name.




Install the PLOS Template
quarto add quarto-journals/plos
quarto use template quarto-journals/plos






NoteWhat this does



This installs a Quarto extension that formats your document to match PLOS journal submission requirements — layout, fonts, and figure formatting. The same approach works for other journal templates under quarto-journals.




Gene Variability Analysis
Copy this into your publication.qmd under ## Gene Variability Analysis:
#| message: false
#| warning: false

gene_data_long <- gene_data %>%
  rename(ensembl_id = `...1`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gene_symbol), gene_symbol != "") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(ensembl_id, gene_symbol),
               names_to = "sample",
               values_to = "expression")

gene_variability <- gene_data_long %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol, ensembl_id) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_expression          = mean(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance                 = var(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    coefficient_of_variation = sd(expression, na.rm = TRUE) / mean_expression,
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

top_genes <- gene_variability %>%
  arrange(desc(variance)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

cat("Total genes analyzed:", nrow(gene_variability), "\n")
cat("Mean variance across all genes:",
    round(mean(gene_variability$variance, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
cat("Most variable gene:", top_genes$gene_symbol[1],
    "with variance =", round(top_genes$variance[1], 2), "\n")

cat("\nTop 10 most variable genes:\n")
print(top_genes %>%
        select(gene_symbol, variance) %>%
        slice_head(n = 10) %>%
        mutate(variance = round(variance, 2)))


Data Visualization
Copy this into your publication.qmd under ## Data Visualization:
#| fig-cap: "Expression heatmap showing scaled expression levels of the
#|   15 most variable genes across all samples. Blue indicates
#|   below-average expression, white indicates average expression,
#|   and red indicates above-average expression for each gene."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

heatmap_data <- gene_data_long %>%
  filter(gene_symbol %in% top_genes$gene_symbol) %>%
  left_join(top_genes %>% select(gene_symbol, variance),
            by = "gene_symbol") %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  mutate(scaled_expr = scale(expression)[, 1]) %>%
  ungroup()

expression_heatmap <- heatmap_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample,
             y = reorder(gene_symbol, variance),
             fill = scaled_expr)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red",
    name = "Scaled\nExpression", limits = c(-3, 3),
    oob = scales::squish
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Expression Variability Heatmap: Top 15 Most Variable Genes",
    subtitle = "Genes ordered by variance (highest at top)",
    x = "Sample ID", y = "Gene Symbol"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, face = "italic"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# print(expression_heatmap)  # not needed when rendering a full .qmd —
# your rendered document and outputs/ folder will show the result

ggsave(paste0("outputs/", timestamp, "_expression_heatmap.png"),
       plot = expression_heatmap, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
Render your publication.qmd document to see your PLOS-formatted article.






TipSaving your figure



The ggsave() call saves a high-resolution .png to your outputs/ folder with a timestamp in the filename — the same automated file naming pattern introduced in Arc 2.

If you don’t have R installed locally, you can run this whole analysis directly in your browser. ggsave() won’t actually save a file here, since this sandbox has no real file system — so print() stays active instead, to show you the plot directly on this page.

Writing Your Own Function
A function has four parts: a name, the [arguments](/glossary.qmd#argument) it accepts, a body of code that runs each time it’s called, and a return value — the thing it hands back to you.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Note About This — Anatomy of a Function





name        <- function(argument1, argument2 = default) {
                 ... body ...
                 return(value)
               }

Name — what you’ll call it by, same rules as naming any object
Arguments — the inputs; can have defaults, so callers only need to supply what’s different each time
Body — the code that runs, using the arguments as temporary objects
Return value — the last line evaluated, or an explicit return() — what the function hands back to whatever called it

This is the DRY principle — Don’t Repeat Yourself. If you find yourself copy-pasting the same calculation more than twice, that’s the signal to wrap it in a function instead.

Turning Your README Into a Living Document
Your README.txt from Arc 2 is a snapshot — accurate the moment you wrote it, and silently out of date the moment your folder structure changes. Converting it to a .qmd file means the project tree inside it can be generated by code instead of typed by hand, so it regenerates itself, correctly, every time you render.

Convert README.txt to README.qmd

Find README.txt in your project folder and rename it to README.qmd (right-click → Rename on Windows, or select the file and press Return on Mac)
If you don’t already have a _quarto.yml file in your project root, create one and add:
project:
  type: default
In your README.qmd, wrap your existing file-structure listing in triple backticks (```) so it’s formatted as a code block
In the terminal, run quarto render, then quarto preview readme.qmd







Note About This — What Is localhost?



The browser window that opens shows an address starting with localhost followed by a port number. That means your own computer is serving the file to itself — it is not on the internet, and no one else can see it. This is how you preview a Quarto document before it’s ever published anywhere.




Automate the Project Tree
Instead of manually retyping your folder structure every time it changes, this code chunk generates and annotates it automatically, every time you render.
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| results: asis

library(fs)

tree_output <- capture.output(dir_tree(".", recurse = 2))

comments <- list(
  "raw_data"       = " (original data goes here)",
  "processed_data" = " (clean data goes here)",
  "scripts"        = " (code goes here)",
  "outputs"        = " (results and charts go here)",
  "README.qmd"     = " (project documentation)"
)

for (item in seq_along(tree_output)) {
  line <- tree_output[item]
  for (name in names(comments)) {
    if (grepl(name, line)) {
      tree_output[item] <- paste0(line, comments[[name]])
      break
    }
  }
}

cat("```\n")
cat(paste(tree_output, collapse = "\n"))
cat("\n```\n")






Note About This — What This Script Does




dir_tree() generates a visual tree of your project folder, two levels deep
capture.output() stores that tree as a character vector your own code can modify — rather than text you’d have to retype by hand
The comments list defines annotations for specific folders or files
The for loop (from Arc 3) checks each line against every name in that list and appends a matching annotation where it finds one
cat() prints the result back out as a formatted code block in your rendered document



Paste this chunk into your README.qmd in place of your plain file tree, wrapped in ```{r} instead of plain triple backticks. Re-render, and your README now regenerates its own project structure every time — try adding your own entry to the comments list and rendering again to see it reflected.

Base R ships with a core set of built-in [functions](/glossary.qmd#function). text:
Two Basic Rules for Writing Reproducible Code

Use # to annotate and document your code. A comment explains why you did something, not just what the code does — that’s the difference between code you can hand to someone else and code only you can decode.
Use a visible pattern to separate sections, e.g. #----- Section Title ------#. This turns a script into something a collaborator — or you, in six months — can scan and navigate without reading every line.

These two habits are the first, smallest form of reproducibility: a reader who wasn’t there when you wrote the code should still be able to follow your thinking.

Caution Code Tour — Why Didn’t My Answer Update?





Change my_age and re-run only this one line:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
birth_year still shows the old value — because R doesn’t recalculate it automatically. It only stores what you told it to store, at the moment you ran that line. The variable has no memory of how it was created, only what it currently holds.
This is a small version of a problem that shows up everywhere in computational work: a pipeline is only as current as the last time each step was actually re-run. Changing one upstream value — a raw data point, a filtering threshold, a parameter — doesn’t automatically update everything downstream of it. You have to re-run the whole chain, in order, every time.
This is why, later in ARCS, you’ll get in the habit of re-running entire scripts top to bottom rather than just the last line you touched — and it’s part of why reproducibility isn’t only “did I get the right answer,” but “would I get the same answer again if I changed one thing and reran everything downstream of it?”









Tip Learn More — Object Naming Rules






Must start with a letter (not a number or symbol)
Can contain letters, numbers, _ and .
Case-sensitive: age and Age are different objects
Avoid names that are already functions in R (e.g. c, mean, data)

text:
Why Version Control?
You’ve probably seen a folder like this:
analysis.R
analysis_v2.R
analysis_final.R
analysis_final_FINAL.R
analysis_final_FINAL_really.R
This is version control done by hand — and it’s painful. You can’t remember what changed between versions, you can’t safely delete any of them, and collaborating means emailing files back and forth.
Git solves this. It’s a time machine for your project: it saves snapshots (called commits) of your work over time, so you can always see what changed, when, and why — and roll back if you need to. Instead of five copies of a file, you keep one file with a complete history.






Note About This — Git vs. GitHub






Git is the tool that tracks changes on your computer (local).
GitHub is a website that hosts git projects online (remote), so you can back them up and share them.

You can use git entirely on its own. GitHub adds the online home.

text:
Local Git in Positron: Modify → Stage → Commit
Your control center for git in Positron is the Source Control tab in the left activity bar. Every change you save to your history goes through three steps:

Modify — you edit files in your project as usual
Stage — you pick which changes to include in the next snapshot
Commit — you save those staged changes as a permanent snapshot

The “stage” step is what surprises newcomers: git lets you choose exactly what goes into each [commit](/glossary.qmd#commit), so you can group related changes together instead of dumping everything at once.
When you change files, they appear in the panel with a letter:



Indicator
Meaning




U
Untracked — a new file git doesn’t know about yet


M
Modified — an existing file has changed


A
Added — a new file that’s been staged, ready to commit









Tip Learn More — Two Zones





The panel has two areas: Changes (modified but not yet staged) and Staged Changes (packed and ready to commit). Clicking the + next to a file moves it from Changes → Staged Changes.




Your First Commit

Look at the Source Control tab. You should see several files listed as untracked (U) — the scripts and data files you’ve worked with so far.
Stage everything. Hover over the Changes heading and click the + icon to stage all files at once. They move into Staged Changes.
Write a commit message. In the message box, type something descriptive: Add project scripts and data.
Commit. Click the ✓ Commit button.







Tip Learn More — Write Messages for Your Future Self





A good commit message finishes the sentence “This commit will…”. Add data loading script is useful; stuff and update are not.





A Second Commit

Make an edit. Open any script and add a comment line at the top:
# Analysis script — tracked with git
Check the panel. The file now shows an M (modified) under Changes.
Review the diff (recommended). Click the filename to open a diff view — additions in green, deletions in red. Reviewing the diff before committing is the single best habit for catching mistakes early.
Stage and commit. Click +, type Add header comment to    analysis script, and click ✓ Commit.







Note About This — A Peek Behind the Curtain





The Source Control panel just runs git commands for you. In the Terminal, run:
git status
git log --oneline
You’ll see the current state and the commits you just made. You never have to use the terminal — but it’s good to know the GUI isn’t doing anything magic. The full command-line workflow is in Extending Further.

title: Arc 6
text:
Excluding Data Files: The .gitignore File






Note About This — Don’t Depend on GitHub for Data Storage





Git is built for code and text, not big datasets — it keeps every version of every file, so a 100 MB dataset can balloon your repo after a few edits, GitHub enforces a 100 MB per-file limit, and git compresses text well but handles large binary data poorly.
But the 100 MB limit is a technical ceiling, not a research-data strategy. A datafile that fits comfortably under it usually still doesn’t belong in a GitHub [repository](/glossary.qmd#repository). If it’s your raw data or your processed data, it needs to be preserved in a [data repository](/glossary.qmd#data-repository): a system built for depositing, citing, and sharing research data (such as Zenodo, OSF, Figshare, or an institutional repository), with different governance structures than a GitHub repo. Arc 8 covers packaging and depositing your data for exactly this reason.



You already have a [].gitignore](/glossary.qmd#gitignore) in your project root — renv::init() created it back in Arc 1 to exclude its package cache. Extend it:

Open it. In Positron’s Explorer pane, click .gitignore in your project root. (If you don’t see it: View → Show Hidden Files.)
Add these lines below what’s already there:
# Ignore data folders
raw_data/
processed_data/

# Ignore large output files
outputs/*.pdf
outputs/*.html
Save the file.
Watch git react. The files in raw_data/ and processed_data/ disappear from the Source Control panel — git is now ignoring them.
Commit the updated .gitignore, with the message Extend .gitignore to exclude data files.







Important Watch Out — Track Code, Not Data





Keep your repository lean by tracking code, not data. This is exactly what the Arc 2 “data management gone awry” story was missing: note where your data actually lives in your README instead of committing it directly.

title: Arc 6
section: Publishing to GitHub with GitHub Desktop
text:
Publishing to GitHub with GitHub Desktop
Your project now has a local history. Let’s give it an online home so it’s backed up and shareable. GitHub Desktop handles authentication through your browser — no SSH keys, no tokens.






Important Watch Out — Make Sure You Have These First






A free GitHub account
GitHub Desktop installed and signed in




Step 1: Sign in to GitHub Desktop

Open GitHub Desktop.
Go to File → Options → Accounts (macOS: GitHub Desktop → Settings → Accounts).
Click Sign in next to GitHub.com. Your browser opens — approve the request, and you’re authenticated.

Step 2: Add your existing project

File → Add Local Repository.
Navigate to your project folder and select it.
Click Add Repository.

GitHub Desktop now shows your project and its full commit history — the same commits you made in Positron.
Step 3: Publish

Click Publish repository at the top.
Confirm the name and add a short description if you like.
Keep this code private — leave this checked for research work (uncheck it only if you intend the project to be public).
Click Publish repository.







Tip Learn More — Positron ↔︎ GitHub Desktop





Keep editing and committing in Positron, then switch to GitHub Desktop and click Push origin to send your latest commits to GitHub. Push whenever you want your online copy up to date.

title: Arc 6
text:
Seeing It on GitHub.com

Go to github.com and open Your repositories.
Click the repository you just published.

You should see all your files, and — by clicking the commits link (or the clock/history icon) — the complete history you built in Positron. Your local project now has an online backup.
Local-first vs. remote-first. There are two ways a project’s life can begin:

Local-first (what we just did): you start on your own computer, build a history, then publish to GitHub — like writing a document on your desktop and later uploading it to share.
Remote-first (cloning): the project already exists on GitHub. You clone it — downloading a complete copy, history and all — before you start working, like a colleague sharing a document you download to edit.







Note About This — When You’ll Use Remote-First





You’ll use the remote-first / clone workflow when collaborating on someone else’s repository — covered in Extending Further, below.

title: Arc 6
section: Extending Further: Collaboration, the Command Line, and Institutional Options
text:
Extending Further: Collaboration, the Command Line, and Institutional Options
This next material goes beyond what we’ll build together today — it’s here so you know it’s possible, and can come back to it on your own.






Caution Code Tour — Collaborating with Fork & Pull Requests





One of the most powerful aspects of version control is collaboration. This walks through a complete, real-world workflow where one person proposes a change to another person’s project.
Roles: the Project Owner owns the original repository and decides what changes to accept; the Contributor wants to suggest improvements, fixes, or additions.
The workflow: Fork → Clone → Branch → Edit → Push → Pull Request.
Fork the repository. On GitHub.com, navigate to the owner’s repository and click Fork — this creates an exact copy of the entire project history, all commits, branches, and files, under your own account. You can experiment freely without affecting the original.
Clone your fork. Click the green <> Code button, copy the HTTPS URL, then in GitHub Desktop: File → Clone Repository, paste the URL, choose a save location, and click Clone.
Create a new branch. In GitHub Desktop, open the Current Branch dropdown → New Branch. Give it a descriptive, lowercase, hyphen-separated, verb-focused name (add-readme-documentation, not new-feature or MyBranch), then Create Branch → Publish branch.
Make your edits in Positron. Click Open in Positron from GitHub Desktop, make your change (a new file, a fix, documentation), and save.
Commit and push. Back in GitHub Desktop, review your changes by clicking each filename, write a descriptive commit message, click Commit to [your-branch-name], then Push origin.
Open a pull request. After pushing, click Create Pull Request. Give it a clear title and a description explaining what changed and why:
## Summary
Added comprehensive README documentation to help users understand
the project's structure, objectives, and prerequisites.

## Changes Made
- Created README.md in the project root
- Documented setup and prerequisites

## Why This Improvement
The repository lacked documentation explaining what it covers and
what participants need to get started.
The owner’s review. On the original repository’s Pull requests tab, open the PR, review line-by-line differences under Files changed (green = additions, red = deletions), leave comments, and either Approve and Merge, Request Changes, or Close without Merging.

Be constructive — focus on the code, not the person
Be specific — point to exact lines and suggest improvements
Be appreciative — thank contributors for their time
Test locally — for important changes, pull the branch and test it yourself before merging

After merging, the owner can safely delete the contributor’s branch; the contributor switches back to main, pulls the latest changes, and deletes their own feature branch — their contribution is now part of the official project history.
Why this matters: the original project is never at risk during development, every change goes through review before integration, contributors and maintainers can discuss openly, and every contribution is documented with clear attribution.









Caution Code Tour — Git on the Command Line





The Positron Source Control panel is a visual interface that runs git commands for you in the background. Here’s how to run those same commands yourself — useful for speed, advanced operations, and remote servers where no GUI is available.
git status
git add .
. means “add all changed files in the current directory and subdirectories.” To stage a single file, name it: git add scripts/analysis.R.
git commit -m "Describe what changed"
git log --oneline
Confirm your data files are actually excluded after adding a .gitignore:
git status --ignored
You should see your data folders listed under “Ignored files.”
If you’ve set up SSH (just below) or an HTTPS credential, you can connect and push from the terminal instead of GitHub Desktop:
git remote add origin git@github.com:username/yourreponame.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main







Approach
Best For




GUI (Source Control panel / GitHub Desktop)
Visual learners, reviewing diffs, getting started


CLI (Terminal)
Speed, advanced operations, remote servers



Many experienced users mix both: GUI for reviewing diffs, CLI for quick commits. On Windows, you may see “CRLF will be replaced by LF the next time Git touches it” — this is normal, git converting Windows-style line endings to Unix-style for consistency, and safe to ignore.









Caution Code Tour — SSH Key Authentication (Advanced)





GitHub Desktop handles authentication for you, so you don’t need this for the core workflow. But if you prefer to push from the command line, SSH keys let you authenticate securely without typing a password every time.
PATs (personal access tokens) are an HTTPS-based alternative, but they expire every 90 days and need renewal. SSH is preferred for long-term research projects because it’s a one-time setup — if SSH is blocked by your network, GitHub Desktop (HTTPS) is the reliable fallback.
Check for existing keys in the Positron Terminal:
ls ~/.ssh
If you see id_ed25519 or id_rsa, you already have keys — skip to adding your key to GitHub, below. Otherwise:

macOS / LinuxWindows


ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
Press Enter to accept the default save location, and again twice to skip a passphrase (optional).
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub


These commands work in the Positron Terminal or Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows) — the Positron Terminal is recommended for consistency.
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"
Press Enter to accept the default save location, and again twice to skip a passphrase (optional).
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa
cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | clip
If clip doesn’t work, run cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub and copy the output manually. If ssh-agent won’t start, try running Positron or Git Bash as Administrator — and if you see “Could not open a connection to your authentication agent,” run ssh-agent bash first, then retry ssh-add.



The .pub file is your public key — safe to share with GitHub. The file without .pub is your private key — never share this. If someone asks for your SSH key, they always mean the public one.
Add it to GitHub: profile photo → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → give it a descriptive title (My Positron Laptop) → paste the key → Add SSH key.
Test the connection:
ssh -T git@github.com
Type yes if prompted about authenticity. You should see: Hi username! You've successfully authenticated...









Tip Learn More — GitHub Enterprise Options at Yale





If you’re working with sensitive research data, Yale offers two GitHub Enterprise options beyond standard GitHub.com.
GitHub Enterprise Server (On-Premises) — a self-hosted platform running within Yale’s secure infrastructure. Suitable for version-controlling analysis scripts, maintaining reproducible research pipelines, and integrating with Yale’s research computing resources. Hosted on Yale’s own infrastructure; supports High data classification (including HIPAA-covered data); full control over data location and security policies.
GitHub Enterprise Cloud — adds advanced functionality to GitHub.com, including SAML single sign-on with Yale credentials, additional GitHub Actions minutes, and enhanced security/compliance features. Cloud-based, managed by GitHub; supports Moderate data classification (not suitable for high-sensitivity data).







Platform
Best For




GitHub.com
Public research, open-source projects, teaching


GitHub Enterprise Cloud
Collaborative research with Yale auth, moderate-sensitivity data


GitHub Enterprise Server
High-sensitivity data, HIPAA compliance, institutional governance



Contact Yale ITS for access, or request GitHub Enterprise support via Yale ServiceNow.
