section: Evaluating AI-Generated Code: A Worked Example
text:
Evaluating AI-Generated Code: A Worked Example
Before you try this yourself, here’s what evaluating AI output actually looks like, step by step. Suppose you’d asked an AI assistant:

“Write an R function that takes a data frame and a column name, and returns the number of values in that column below 10.”

And it handed back this:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
It runs. It returns a number. Is that enough?






Note About This — The AI Code Checklist





Run this same checklist on every piece of AI-generated code before it goes anywhere near a real analysis — all five items are habits this course has already built, just aimed at a new source of code:

Does it run? — the lowest bar, and the only one an AI’s confidence guarantees.
Do you understand every line? — if not, that’s the signal to ask the AI to explain it, not to accept it on faith (Arc 3: reading error messages applies here too, since you can’t debug what you don’t understand).
Is it documented in your words — your Quarto doc explaining what it does and why, independent of whatever comments the AI added itself? (Arc 2)
Is it committed, with a message describing what changed and why? (Arc 6)
Does renv::snapshot() capture every package it pulled in — not just the ones you already had? (Arc 1)

Running the example above through this list: it executes (1), it’s simple enough to understand fully (2) — but it silently drops every NA without flagging that it did, which is exactly the Arc 3 lesson about na.rm and missing values resurfacing in new clothes. An AI didn’t know to ask whether that silence was intentional. You have to.




Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: Arc 7
section: Your Turn: Get Code From an AI, Then Audit It
text:
Your Turn: Get Code From an AI, Then Audit It
Open Claude, ChatGPT, or whichever assistant you use, and ask it this:

“Write an R function called flag_mid_expression that takes a data frame, a column name, a low threshold, and a high threshold, and returns TRUE for every value strictly between the two thresholds — and FALSE for everything else, including missing values.”

Paste whatever it gives you into the cell below, in place of the placeholder, and run it.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now run it through the checklist above. Specifically:

Does it correctly return FALSE — not NA — for missing values? (anyNA(raw_data$GSM3119015) told you there’s at least one to test this against.)
Do you understand every operator it used?
Could you explain, out loud, what this function does to someone who’s never seen it?



One possible correct version

flag_mid_expression <- function(df, col_name, low, high) {
  values <- df[[col_name]]
  result <- values > low & values < high
  result[is.na(values)] <- FALSE
  result
}
Many AI assistants will skip the NA handling entirely — > and < against NA silently return NA, not FALSE. If what you pasted did that, you’ve just caught exactly the kind of error this checklist exists to catch.







Caution Code Tour — Three Ways AI-Generated R Code Fails Quietly





Three real patterns worth recognizing on sight. Each runs if you run it in your own browser cell — try each one before reading what’s wrong.
1. The invented function. AI assistants sometimes blend real function names with plausible-sounding ones that don’t exist:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This fails loudly — could not find function — which is actually the easy case. The real function is mean(x, na.rm = TRUE); mean_no_na() was never real.
2. The misordered argument. Unlike many functions, grepl() expects pattern first, text to search second — reverse them and the function still runs, it just silently matches nothing:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Compare the two outputs. The first returns all FALSE. Nothing about that result looks like an error.
3. The outdated package. Ask an AI for a “group and summarize” operation in R and it may reach for the plyr package — a real tool, but one dplyr (which this course has used throughout Arc 5) has almost entirely replaced:
#| eval: false
library(plyr)
ddply(raw_metadata, "genotype", summarise, n = length(genotype))
This isn’t wrong, exactly — it’s dated. plyr is no longer actively maintained, and its functions can conflict with dplyr if both are loaded. The equivalent you already know:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
An AI trained on years of public code will sometimes hand you the 2014 answer to a question that has a better 2024 answer.









Tip Learn More — Getting Better Code Out of an AI





A vague prompt gets a vague — or wrong — answer. A few habits that consistently produce better code:

Be specific about shape and edge cases — “returns FALSE for missing values” is something you have to ask for; it’s rarely assumed.
Give it real context — paste the actual column names or a few real rows, instead of describing your data in the abstract.
Ask it to explain its own code back to you — if the explanation doesn’t match what the code actually does, that mismatch is worth investigating before you trust either one.
Treat the first answer as a draft — asking a follow-up (“what happens here if the column has an NA?”) often surfaces exactly the kind of gap this arc has been pointing at.

For more on getting useful results from Claude specifically, Anthropic’s prompting documentation is at docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview.









Tip Learn More — Going Further: Claude Code





Everything in this arc used chat-based AI — you asked a question, got code back, and pasted it in yourself. A coding agent like Claude Code goes a step further: it reads your project’s files directly, writes code into them, runs it, and fixes its own errors. The checklist from this arc doesn’t change — it’s the same “Claude does, you decide” split — it just needs sharper tools, since an agent can do far more per turn than a chat window ever could. ARCS’s companion class, Analyzing Research Data with Claude Code, walks through exactly that: permission rules that enforce what advice alone can’t, a plan-before-you-code workflow, and a required human review step before anything is trusted. If this arc made you want to go further, that’s the natural next stop.

title: Arc 8
section: Packaging Your Project for Someone Else
text:
Packaging Your Project for Someone Else
Every arc so far has quietly been building toward this moment. The README you were asked to write in Arc 1, the file naming conventions from Arc 2, the .gitignore and commit history from Arc 6 — all of it is exactly what a real data or code repository asks you to produce at deposit time. There’s no new skill left to learn here. There’s just a new name for what you’ve already been doing: packaging.






Important Watch Out — This Isn’t About Picking a Repository





We won’t be creating a Zenodo account or clicking through a real repository deposit form today. The specific repository you’ll eventually use depends on your field, your funder, and your data — that’s a decision for later, with your librarian. What matters today is the shape of what every deposit process asks for, so none of it is a surprise when you actually need it.




Your README Already Covers Tier One
Arc 1 and Arc 4 already walked you through writing and maintaining a README. That’s still the first thing any repository will look for, and nothing about it changes here — if you want a refresher, the checklist is back in those two arcs. What’s worth asking now is: is a README always enough?


A Second Tier: The Codebook
A README describes your project. A codebook describes your columns — what each one means, what unit it’s in, and why a value might be missing. It’s the next thing a repository asks for after the README, and most of it can be generated instead of typed by hand:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Note About This — Generated, Then Finished by Hand





purrr::map_chr() and purrr::map_dbl() — functions you already loaded with tidyverse in Arc 5 — can tell you a column’s type and how many values are missing automatically. They cannot tell you what a column means or why a value is missing. A codebook is always partly generated, partly irreducibly human — much like the AI-generated code from Arc 7, it still needs someone who understands the data to finish the job.





When a Repository Wants More Than a Codebook
Some repositories go one step further and ask for structural metadata — not just what each column means, but how separate files relate to each other. You’ve already built this, without the name attached to it. Back in Arc 5:
clean_data <- clean_data %>%
  select(all_of(clean_meta_data$sample_id))

setequal(clean_meta_data$sample_id, colnames(clean_data))
That join is structural metadata — a scripted, verifiable statement of exactly how clean_data and clean_meta_data relate. Some repository formats (datapackage.json from the Frictionless Data standard; SDRF, used by expression-data archives like ArrayExpress) ask you to write that relationship down explicitly, in a file, rather than leave it implicit in a script. Not every repository requires this — the data-repository world is far less standardized than the code-package world is right now. But if one ever does ask, you’ll recognize what it’s asking for, because you already built the relationship it wants described.


Documenting Your Environment, Automatically
A README can describe your setup in prose. R can also just tell you exactly what it was, with no risk of the description drifting out of sync with reality:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This single function call — R version, operating system, every loaded package and its exact version — is the kind of thing a real data package often asks you to include directly, sometimes as its own file (sessionInfo.txt or similar). It’s renv’s snapshot, read back to you in plain language.


Citing a Dataset the Way You Cite a Package

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Run this, and look closely: R has been generating a properly formatted, machine-readable citation for every package you’ve loaded this entire course — most people never look. A DOI does the same job for data that a citation does for code: a stable, resolvable name. Your own dataset already has one. A one-line “how to cite this” entry for your own README might read:

Data: GSE113754, NIH Gene Expression Omnibus. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE113754







Note About This — Citable, Not Just Downloadable





A repository deposit usually earns a DOI — a permanent link that won’t break even if the file moves, gets renamed, or the hosting service redesigns its site. That permanence is what lets someone else cite your data the same way they’d cite a paper.









Tip Learn More — Where This Actually Goes






Zenodo — general-purpose, issues a DOI, widely accepted by funders and journals
OSF — project-level, good for packaging code, data, and materials together
Figshare — similar to Zenodo, popular in some fields over others

Most funders and journals also now require a data availability statement in the manuscript — where the underlying data lives and how to access it. If your field has a standard, field-specific repository instead (a gene expression database for genomics, for instance), that often takes priority over a general-purpose one. Your library’s research data services can help you figure out which applies.




Everything above assumes that once a project is ready to share, sharing it fully is the goal. For a public mouse dataset, that assumption holds. It does not hold universally — and knowing when it doesn’t is part of reproducible practice, not an exception to it.

title: Arc 8
text:
The Limits of Reproducibility
Back in Arc 2, before any of this started, we put up a list:

R’s Flexibility Creates New Responsibilities

Efficiency — You can still write code that runs slowly
Best practices — R is agnostic to readability, optimal analysis, data ethics
Data management — Explicit instructions are needed to select and organize pipelines, folders, files
Information — Code that runs is not always code that produces desired or understandable results


Seven arcs later, you can read every line of that list and name exactly which habit answers it. There’s a fifth item that was never on that list, because no habit in this course resolves it the way renv resolves efficiency or .gitignore resolves data management:

Who the data is about, and who gets to decide how it’s used.







Important Watch Out — Reproducible Isn’t the Same as Right





A perfectly reproducible pipeline — pinned packages, committed history, documented every step — can still analyze the wrong population, apply the wrong definition, or answer a question nobody should have asked, with full fidelity, every single time it’s run. Running the same flawed analysis twice and getting the same flawed answer twice is not a correction. It’s a well-documented mistake.




A Live Example of This Exact Trap
ARCS’s companion extension, Analyzing Research Data with Claude Code, walks through a real version of this. Students there ask an AI coding agent to estimate a published health statistic, and compare what happens when a single hidden decision changes — not a bug, just a quiet choice about how to handle a missing survey answer. The script still runs without error. It’s still fully reproducible — anyone re-running it gets the identical number back. But depending on that one choice, the result ranges from roughly 48% to over 90%, for the same underlying data. That extension calls this the garden of forking paths: when it’s cheap to try “just one more” version of a definition, and you report the version you like best, reproducibility doesn’t save you — it just means your selectively chosen answer is now permanently, verifiably reproducible.


Sometimes the Responsible Move Is to Share Less
Two concrete cases where limiting sharing — on purpose — is the correct call, not a gap in your packaging:






Caution Code Tour — Anonymization Is a Reproducibility Tradeoff, Not a Failure






Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
A README that documents why a column was generalized is doing its job correctly — a stranger who can’t reconstruct your exact original data is sometimes exactly what responsible sharing looks like.



Code and data can also follow different rules entirely. A project folder can be fully honest about this:
project/
├── README.md              ← includes a Data Access section
├── data/
│   ├── raw_data/           ← empty; .gitignore'd on purpose
│   └── data_access.md      ← "Raw data available by request under DUA #XXXX"
├── scripts/                ← fully public, unchanged
└── outputs/                ← fully public, unchanged
Your analysis pipeline — everything this course has built — can often be fully public even when the data it ran on cannot be. “Data available by request under a data use agreement; code available here” is a complete, honest package. It is not a lesser one.






Note About This — FAIR and CARE Principles





The slides for this arc laid out FAIR and CARE side by side. The short version: FAIR asks whether data can be found and reused. CARE asks whether it should be — and who gets to answer that. A dataset can score perfectly on every FAIR criterion and still have been collected, shared, or reused in a way the people it describes never consented to. The anonymization example above is a CARE decision wearing a FAIR-looking folder.









Important Watch Out — What Are You Pasting Into an AI Tool?





Arc 7 asked whether you could trust code an AI handed you. This is the same question, aimed the other direction: what are you handing an AI? Pasting study data into a general AI chat tool is a data-sharing decision, even when it doesn’t feel like one. Institutional tools — Yale’s Clarity portal, for instance, which keeps data encrypted on-prem — change the security profile. They don’t make the CARE question disappear just because the server is local.





Where This Leaves You
There’s no function call, no package, no checklist item that resolves “should this be reproduced at all?” That question doesn’t go away because you’ve finished a course. Computational reproducibility is necessary for trustworthy science. It has never been sufficient — a perfectly reproducible pipeline can still answer the wrong question, on the wrong data, without the right permission to ask it. No package, pin, or commit history will tell you that on its own. That part stays on you.

title: Arc 7
text:
A New Kind of Collaborator

You will write code with an AI’s help — maybe you already do.
That’s not a problem this course is trying to talk you out of.
The problem is narrower: code that runs isn’t the same as code you understand, can verify, and can hand to someone else.

title: Arc 7
text:
Runs ≠ Correct

An AI assistant can hand you a function that executes without error and returns the wrong answer.
It can invent a function that doesn’t exist, reorder a real function’s arguments, or quietly reach for an outdated package.
None of these mistakes announce themselves — they look exactly as confident as a correct answer.

title: Arc 7
text:
The Checklist Doesn’t Change

Does it run?
Do you understand every line?
Is it documented in your words?
Is it committed?
Does renv::snapshot() capture what it pulled in?


Five habits this course already built. Only the source of the code is new.


This is the first exercise in the series that sends students to an outside tool and back — their own AI assistant, not a browser cell. Some will get back code with an obvious, easy-to-catch error; others will get back something subtler, or something that’s actually fine. Have a version of each ready to discuss if the room’s results don’t split that way on their own.

title: Arc 7
text:
Three Quiet Failure Modes

The invented function — fails loudly, the easy case
The misordered argument — runs, finds nothing, looks fine
The outdated package — not wrong, just dated


None of these announce themselves. That’s the point.

text:
A Policy Still Being Written

In December 2025, NIH proposed a new rule: imaging of the human face or head — CT, MRI, even 3D reconstructions — now counts as a biometric identifier, requiring controlled access.
Why now? Because researchers showed facial-recognition models could re-identify “de-identified” MRI scans from the 3D shape of a skull alone.
This policy isn’t settled. It’s a public comment period, open right now, catching up to a technical reality.

The Point Isn’t This Specific Rule

The point is that what counts as “appropriately shared” keeps changing — and it changes because someone found a new way to extract identity from data that looked safe.
Our dataset is public mouse RNA-seq. No human subject, no biometric risk. But the habit this should build applies regardless of your field: the norms for sharing data responsibly are still being written, in your discipline too.
Today has two halves: packaging a project for someone else to use, and asking whether — and how much — it should be used.

Beyond FAIR: Who the Data Is About









FAIR asks
CARE asks




Collective Benefit
Is it Findable, Accessible?
Does reuse benefit the community the data describes?


Authority to Control
Is it Interoperable?
Who has standing to decide reuse — not just who holds the file?


Responsibility
Is it Reusable?
Does reuse — including by an AI tool — risk harm no one anticipated?


Ethics
—
Should this be reproduced at all?




FAIR describes the shape of good data management. CARE asks a question FAIR never does: not just can this be reused, but should it be, and by whose permission.
